transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Lina Park (Redwood AE), Mateo Ruiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (CTO, Veridian), Ben Meyer (ML Eng), Samir Patel (Platform)
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/rec/ff-20251107-verd-128k-rtd-001

Auto-generated Summary: (may be incomplete)
- Focus on long-context strategies for 128k+ prompts, chunking and recombination approaches, KV cache sizing and eviction policies, batching and throughput tuning, and quantization options for cost/latency.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lina: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros then we'll jump into the 128k deep dive.
[00:18] Aisha: Hi, Aisha here, CTO at Veridian Health. We're really focused on running long patient records in inference, so privacy is a big thing — PHI, encryption, all that.
[00:27] Ben: Ben — ML eng, mostly model infra. We have concerns around latency spikes when sequence goes long and also tokenization chunking behavior.
[00:35] Samir: Samir — platform. We run in a VPC, KMS keys are required, and we want to understand what private deployment looks like versus dedicated.
[00:45] Mateo: Great, thanks. Today's agenda: we'll cover how Redwood's runtime handles extremely long contexts (128k+), KV-cache mechanics, chunking strategies (sliding windows vs chunk+rerank), batching implications, quantization options, and ops around VPC/on-prem.

[02:10] Lina: One quick question — what's your success criteria? Latency p95? Cost per request? Throughput?
[02:18] Aisha: Primary is p95 latency under 2s for most interactive queries across a 128k fetch, but we also have nightly batch jobs where throughput matters more and latency can be higher. Security trumps cost, but cost can't be astronomical.

[05:05] Mateo: Okay, so starting with KV cache: our runtime keeps a distributed KV cache per model shard to avoid re-computing prefixes. For 128k+ contexts the advice is to do prefix pre-computation where possible and keep hot prefixes pinned in memory. Note: with very high sequence lengths you may hit GPU memory constraints; we support chunked KV eviction policies and local SSD spill for Dedicated/Private.
[05:40] Ben: Can you clarify "pinning" — does that mean we reserve memory on a dedicated pool? Because we run multi-tenant workloads in dedicated right now.
[05:49] Mateo: Pinning is a config on Dedicated — you can reserve a slice of KV memory for customer prefixes. For Private, you control nodes and can allocate bigger KV cache. In hosted mode, we do best-effort and fall back to chunking.

[07:12] Ben: How about chunking strategies — we've tried sliding-window attention and simple chunk+overlap; both had quality drop-offs.
[07:20] Mateo: Right, there are tradeoffs. We typically recommend hybrid chunking: semantic chunk boundaries (paragraph/section-aware) + overlap of 1-2k tokens with a recombination step that does reranking using a short cross-attention pass. That minimizes context loss versus naive windows.
[07:58] Aisha: Does Redwood provide tooling to auto-chunk based on anchors or headings?
[08:05] Mateo: Yes, we have a chunker utility in the SDK that can do rule-based and embedding-based chunking. It outputs chunks with metadata to help reassemble. We'll share a sample. Link: https://redwood.ai/sdk/chunker-samples

[09:40] Samir: From infra side, we need to understand throughput. If we pin KV and have big chunks, how does batching interact?
[09:49] Mateo: Batching is tricky with large KV footprints. We do continuous batching where requests are batched in the decoder loop to fill GPU work without reloading KV each time. For peak throughput it's better to group similar sequence lengths and use dynamic padding. Our profiler shows that grouping by sequence bucket reduces wasted compute.
[10:30] Ben: Any hard numbers? Like tokens/sec for 1x V100-ish or A10?
[10:36] Mateo: Numbers vary but ballpark: on A100-class hardware with optimized kernels and 4-bit quantization, you can see O(50-150) tokens/sec per GPU for very long contexts depending on batch shape. For 128k end-to-end workloads a lot depends on the amount of recomputation — so microbenchmarks are key.

[12:45] Lina: Let's talk quantization. We heard about Q4 and Q5 — what's Redwood supporting and what are the perf/quality tradeoffs?
[12:53] Mateo: We support several quantization profiles. Q8 is safe and close to FP16 in quality for many models, Q4 mixes are possible with some accuracy regressions in sensitive tasks. For long-context tasks we're cautious: lower-bit quant can amplify attention noise for low-probability token scoring. We recommend running your evals; Redwood Optimize can auto-suggest quant profiles per workload.
[13:36] Ben: So for PHI extraction we should maybe stick to Q8?
[13:39] Mateo: That's the conservative approach. If you care about inference cost and can accept a small drop, Q4 evals may pass — but test on your prompts.

[15:00] Aisha: About attention optimizations — flash attention, block-sparse, linear attention — which ones are in the runtime?
[15:08] Mateo: We support FlashAttention and kernel fusions for causal attention, and we have experimental support for block-sparse and locality-biased attention for very long sequences. FlashAttention helps memory bandwidth and reduces GPU memory, making 128k more feasible. Block-sparse can reduce compute but often requires model-aware fine-tuning.

[17:20] Ben: Any gotchas with flash attention and quantization combined?
[17:26] Mateo: Yes — some FlashAttention kernels expect FP16 or BF16 math; mixing with int8/4 quant flows needs shim layers. Our runtime routes kernels based on both model dtype and quant profile to avoid incorrect math. Small transcription note: I said "shim" but the transcript probably shows "sham" in automated text.

[19:00] Samir: For Private deployment, what's the KMS story? We must use our HSM-backed keys and restrict egress.
[19:07] Mateo: Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations. Keys never leave the customer control plane; we integrate with your KMS for envelope encryption. Egress can be locked down — also audit logs are shipped to your SIEM via syslog or S3. We'll include our security integration doc.

[21:30] Aisha: On compliance, SOC2 and ISO — do you have attestation? We need to surface to our compliance folks.
[21:37] Lina: Yes, we have SOC2 Type II and ISO attestation for the control plane, and Private deployments can be run entirely in customer env for attestation. We'll send the artifacts.

[24:05] Ben: Back to performance — if a request needs to look at full 128k context, is the recommendation to stream chunks to the model and then do a final cross-attention pass?
[24:14] Mateo: Correct. Typical pattern: 1) chunk and encode prefixes (embedding/encoder step), 2) maintain KV store for each chunk, 3) for a query, run short cross-attention over chunk summaries or use a retriever to identify top K relevant chunks, 4) do focused cross-attention and reranking. For some retrieval-heavy workloads you can avoid touching full context live.

[27:00] Ben: We heard about continuous KV caching — what's the eviction policy? LRU? LFU?
[27:06] Mateo: We offer pluggable policies: LRU by default, but you can opt for frequency-based (LFU) or TTL-based eviction. For health records we usually recommend TTL+pinning for recent records then LFU for older history.

[29:30] Aisha: Cost estimate ballpark for running 128k queries at scale? We're trying to weigh Dedicated vs Private vs hosted.
[29:38] Lina: We'll build a custom cost model but rough guidance: Dedicated can be cheaper per-token if you commit capacity and can amortize KV memory. Private has higher upfront infra cost but predictable ops. Hosted is fastest to start but may be more expensive at scale and you need to accept shared infra policies. We'll send a TCO spreadsheet.

[31:50] Samir: Is there tooling to visualize per-token cost and where time is spent?
[31:56] Mateo: Yes, Redwood Console has per-token latency/cost breakdown, route-level dashboards, and a trace that shows time in KV lookup, attention kernels, and decode. We'll include screenshots.

[34:10] Ben: A couple edge cases: what about long-lived KV entries and model updates — how do you handle warm caches across model rollouts?
[34:18] Mateo: We have a rollouts mechanism: canary + gradual migration with cache replay. For major model changes we recommend re-encoding critical prefixes as a batch job. We also support dual-serving where old and new models run and we compare outputs.

[37:00] Aisha: How invasive is the on-prem agent — firewall rules, ports?
[37:07] Mateo: For Private on-prem, the control plane can be air-gapped; the runtime nodes need minimal outbound for package updates optionally. We'll provide a firewall rules doc. For VPC-hosted Private the egress is limited and we support NAT configurations.

[40:25] Ben: Are there customer references running 100k+ contexts in production?
[40:31] Lina: We have a few customers (health and legal) running long contexts; we can make intros if needed.

[42:00] Mateo: Quick demo snippet — I'm going to show a profiler output (screen share). Note: automated transcript probably drops some of the code references.
[42:12] Mateo: (screen) Here you can see kernel time vs KV lookup time. For this workload most time is in attention kernels until sequence grows beyond 64k where KV IO starts to matter.
[44:50] Ben: If we want to run a PoC, what's the minimal setup?
[44:56] Lina: For a PoC we suggest: provide a representative sample of records and expected queries, decide deployment mode (Dedicated recommended for performance parity), we'll run a 128k benchmark on your sample, then review accuracy/latency. If good, we can expand to a longer pilot.

[46:10] Aisha: Any data residency problems with Hosted? We need PHI to stay in region.

[46:16] Lina: Our hosted API supports region pinning for data residency. But for strict PHI restrictions Private is recommended.

[48:00] Mateo: One more technical note on chunk recombination: when reranking we often use a lightweight cross-encoder at 1-2k tokens to produce final scores — cheaper than full decode across 128k. Also use retrieval-augmented generation patterns to keep live model context small.

[50:15] Ben: For quantization tooling, can we run automated A/B evals across gold prompts?
[50:21] Mateo: Yes, Redwood Optimize has eval harnesses that run against prompt suites and report regressions. We'll run your PHI extraction set across Q8 and Q4 and show delta metrics.

[52:40] Samir: On the ops side, what happens under overload — graceful degradation?
[52:46] Mateo: We have routing policies: fall back to faster model variants, serve a summary-only response, or queue requests with SLA-based prioritization. For Dedicated you can configure burst capacity and automatic fallback.

[55:00] Aisha: Ok let's recap and next steps.
[55:05] Lina: Recap: Redwood will run a 128k benchmark with Veridian samples (Mateo), send security artifacts and pricing (Lina), customer to provide sample data profile (Ben/Samir). We'll schedule an in-person lab test if benchmark looks promising.
[55:25] Ben: Sounds good. One ask — please include exact kernel/hardware details for the benchmark so we can compare with our infra.
[55:33] Mateo: Will do — include A100/A10 numbers and kernel versions.
[56:00] Aisha: Thanks all. We'll review the security docs and reconvene after the benchmark.
[56:08] Lina: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes and next steps.

End of transcript. Some ASR artifacts present (names and acronyms occasionally mis-transcribed).
